subject: FalconBridge connector design — SDK auth, routing, structured tool calls and fallback strategy
messages:
From: Alyssa Park <alyssa.park@falconbridge.com>
To: Ava Chen <ava_chen@redwood.com>
Cc: Luke Carter <l.carter@falconbridge.com>
Date: 2028-07-18 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Follow-up: connector options and quick wins from today's call

Hi Ava —

Thanks again for the call this morning. Helpful recap: FalconBridge wants a low-friction POC to validate: (1) SDK onboarding and auth patterns, (2) routing between regional models for latency/cost, (3) invoking external tools (payments API / inventory lookup) via function/tool calling, and (4) boosting retrieval quality with embeddings + reranker.

Can you send a concise design recommendation we can review with our eng and security teams? Items we especially care about: SDK install and example auth flows (API key vs OIDC), expected network flows for tool calls (are tool calls proxied through Redwood or sent directly from our backend?), recommended structured-output schema for safe tool invocation, and a clear fallback strategy if a tool errors (e.g., retry, degrade to cached answer, or reroute).

I'll attach FalconBridge's security questionnaire — we need answers for the security lead before internal sign-off. Also include an estimated timeline for a 2-week sandbox POC (who needs access and what we need to deliver).

Thanks,
Alyssa
Alyssa Park
Director of Platform Engineering
FalconBridge

Attachments: falconbridge-security-questions.pdf (survey, 16 pages)

From: Ava Chen <ava_chen@redwood.com>
To: Alyssa Park <alyssa.park@falconbridge.com>
Cc: Luke Carter <l.carter@falconbridge.com>, Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-07-18 10:48:00 -07:00
Subject: RE: Follow-up: connector options and quick wins from today's call

Hi Alyssa — thanks for the clear ask and the questionnaire. Below is a compact recommendation meant to be consumable by your eng + security teams; I listed next steps at the end. We can expand any section into a short runbook or diagrams if useful.

1) SDK & auth (quickstart)
- Use Redwood's client SDK (JS/TS + Python sample). For a sandbox POC, API key auth is fastest: create a scoped API key with read/write-permissions for the dedicated sandbox model.
- For production, we recommend OIDC + short-lived tokens (our SDK supports token refresh via a client-side callback). We support JWK validation and can integrate with your IdP (Okta/Azure AD).
- Example flow: Your backend exchanges OIDC code -> obtains short-lived Redwood token -> calls Redwood inference endpoints. Avoid embedding long-lived keys in user browsers.

2) Routing & model selection
- Policy-based routing: start with simple ruleset: region (us-east/us-west) -> model tier (latency-sensitive / cost-optimized).
- We recommend pinning the core intents to a low-latency variant and allowing a cost-optimized fallback for batch jobs.

3) Tool / function calling (design & structured output)
- Tool defs: represent tools as typed manifests (name, inputs schema, allowed_side_effects, timeout_ms). Example: inventory_lookup({sku: string}) -> {qty, location}.
- Structured output: use a strict JSON schema returned by the model to indicate tool invocation; e.g., {"action":"call_tool","tool":"inventory_lookup","args":{...}}. Redwood SDK includes a validator to reject malformed tool calls before execution.
- Proxy vs direct: For POC, proxying tool calls through your backend is simplest (better control & audit). For low-latency, you can implement signed webhook endpoints so Redwood can call restricted tools directly; requires mTLS or signed JWTs.

4) Parallel tools & error handling
- Parallelism: allow a small bounded fanout (we suggest max 3 parallel tool invocations for POC). This gives latency benefits while keeping cost predictable.
- Error strategy: implement a circuit-breaker per-tool + exponential backoff. If all parallel calls fail, fallback order: cached response -> approximate (embedding-based) rerank -> gracefully decline with a clarifying question.
- Idempotency: require tools to support idempotency keys for side-effecting ops.

5) Embeddings + reranker
- Retrieval flow: embed query -> nearest-neighbor fetch (top 10) -> cross-encoder rerank on top 3. For POC, we recommend using Redwood-hosted embeddings and an on-prem nearest-neighbor index (we can help set this up).
- Quality guardrails: add a relevance threshold and a fallback to a curated FAQ set if confidence is low.

6) Operational considerations
- Observability: Redwood Console provides token-level cost/lambda breakdown per tool-route and per-request traces. We'll hand over a dashboard for the POC.
- Security: we can mark the sandbox with VPC egress rules and short retention for logs.

Attachments included: redwood-connector-checklist.xlsx, connector-manifest-proposal.pdf (sample manifests + schema).

Next steps / timeline (proposed 2-week POC)
- Day 0-1: Redwood creates sandbox project and scoped API keys; FalconBridge shares a test service account.
- Day 2-4: SDK onboarding + sample tool manifests, one sample tool proxied via FalconBridge backend (inventory_lookup).
- Day 5-8: Implement parallel call prototype (max fanout=3), circuit-breaker, and embedding+rerank baseline.
- Day 9-10: Validation with FalconBridge QA + security Q&A.
- Day 11-14: Joint demo, handover notes, SOW for next phase.

Please confirm who on your side should get the sandbox keys and whether you prefer proxy-only calls for the POC. Happy to jump on a 30-minute sync if needed.

Best,
Ava Chen
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Subject: RE: Follow-up: connector options and quick wins from today's call

Quick technical notes from infra side (calling out tradeoffs):

- Caching: prefer prefix/KV caching for predictable latency on common queries (inventory/status). Cache invalidation is the hardest bit — recommend TTL + webhook-based invalidation from FalconBridge when inventory changes.
- Batching: for high-throughput retrievals use continuous batching inside Redwood runtime. For POC keep explicit batch size small to reduce latency variance.
- Fanout limit rationale: each parallel tool call amplifies cost and concurrency; starting at 3 lets us measure tail latency and error amplification. If tool calls are local and very cheap, we can increase later.
- Fallback detail: when fallback to embedding-rerank is used, label the source ("heuristic_rerank") in the response so downstream consumers can treat it differently.
- Security: for direct callbacks, use mTLS client certs or short-lived signed JWTs. For proxying, we recommend request-scoped auth tokens and retention-limited logs.

If FalconBridge wants a reference manifest, I attached a very small example in the connector-manifest-proposal.pdf (see the "inventory_lookup" example). Happy to PR a sample SDK snippet into our docs repo for the POC.

-Aditya

Thanks Ava / Aditya — this is exactly the level of detail we needed. A few quick confirmations:

- For the POC we'll take proxy-only tool calls initially. That avoids extra network approvals while we validate semantics.
- Please provision the sandbox project and create two scoped API keys: one for our backend (server) and one for a CI test runner. Who should I send the service account details to?
- We've attached the security questionnaire to this reply; can you mark where you need additional artifacts (SOC2 report, network diagrams, key rotation policy)?
- On timelines: target start next Monday (2028-07-24). Can Redwood share the HubSpot SOW link and a DocuSign draft for the POC SOW?

We'll get Luke (integration owner) and James (procurement) looped in after you provision the sandbox. If everything looks good we'll confirm the kickoff by Friday.
